query: Starting from crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals, what single intervention could overcome the unresolved risk of structural or chemical instability during operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the mechanism by which it would preserve stability, the predicted outcome relative to the same nanoparticles without the intervention, relevant temperature, time, and compositional boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a thermal-exposure experiment with measurements and failure criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The structural or chemical instability of crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals during operation in the 773-1173 K catalytic regime can be overcome by a single intervention of disorder-to-order phase transition via Joule heating for a short period of time (~5 min) followed by rapid cooling (~10^4 K/s).
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals
generation.intervention: Disorder-to-order phase transition via Joule heating for a short period of time (~5 min) followed by rapid cooling (~10^4 K/s)
generation.mechanism: The disorder-to-order phase transition stabilizes the nanoparticles by reducing the configurational entropy and increasing the thermal stability, as evidenced by records PMC6728353 and PMC9260516. The mechanism is derived from materials-science principles and supported by records PMC8797181 and PMC10466320.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved structural and chemical stability of the nanoparticles during operation in the 773-1173 K catalytic regime
generation.baseline: Crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals without the intervention
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature and time conditions for the disorder-to-order phase transition may vary depending on the specific composition and crystal structure of the nanoparticles

falsification_experiment.design: Thermal-exposure experiment with measurements of structural and chemical stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles exhibit significant structural or chemical instability during operation in the 773-1173 K catalytic regime after the intervention, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles (NPs) have attracted significant attention as promising catalysts owing to the various unique synergistic effects originating from the nanometer-scale, near-equimolar mixing of five or more components to produce single-phase solid solutions. However, the study of sub-nanometer HEA clusters having sizes of less than 1 nm remains incomplete despite the possibility of novel functions related to borderline molecular states with discrete quantum energy levels. The present work demonstrates the synthesis of CeO2 nanorods (CeO2-NRs) on which sub-nanometer CoNiCuZnPd HEA clusters were formed with the aid of a pronounced hydrogen spillover effect on readily reducible CeO2 (110) facets. The CoNiCuZnPd HEA sub-nanoclusters exhibited higher activity during the reduction of NO by H2 even at low temperatures compared with the corresponding monometallic catalysts. These clusters also showed a unique structural reversibility in response to repeated exposure to oxidative/reductive conditions, based on the sacrificial oxidation of the non-noble metals. In summary, we report the first synthesis of MPEI nanoparticles with up to eight constituent elements through a unique disorder-to-order phase transition. This transition is achieved by starting with disordered, solid-solution HEA nanoparticles that are Joule-heated for a short period of time (~5 min) followed by rapid cooling (~104 K/s). The HEA starting materials synthesized through a rapid thermal shock (tens of milliseconds heating) enables the mixing of the diverse elements, regardless of their thermodynamic miscibility. The subsequent ~5 min of heating is then critical to achieve the disorder-to-order transition that converts the HEA nanoparticles into MPEI nanoparticles, which is driven by thermodynamic stability. In addition, the limited heating time and the ensuing rapid temperature quenching prevent the MPEI nanoparticles from excessive growth and agglomeration. This unique approach not only produces stable MPEIs at the nanoscale but also can enable previously unidentified MPEI compositions (e.g., PtPdAuFeCoNiCuSn) that have never been achieved by traditional methods because of the inherent immiscibility of the elements. In this paper, small PtPdCoCuNi HEA nanoparticles were successfully prepared by a one-pot solvothermal synthesis method and deposited on SiO2 to prepare a PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst with uniform dispersion of HEA nanoparticles. The catalytic performance of the PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst for nitrobenzene hydrogenation was tested and compared to counterparts with fewer metal components. The PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst exhibits high activity even at room temperature. The catalyst was characterized by a series of techniques, including HRSTEM, XRD, XPS, and DRIFTS, to obtain mechanistic understanding of the structure–activity relationship of the HEA catalyst. Both experimental and theoretical results evidence the formation of isolated Pt and Pd active sites in HEA and the resulting charge-transfer from the cheap transition metals to the noble metals, which suggests that the modulated electronic structure could promote adsorption of nitrobenzene on Pt/Pd active sites and eventually enhance nitrobenzene hydrogenation activity.
